title: Electrochemistry and redox
note: Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode, in every kind of cell. In a galvanic cell a spontaneous reaction sends electrons through a wire from anode to cathode; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and E°cell > 0 means spontaneous. ΔG° = −nFE°cell links voltage to free energy. In electrolysis, charge (current × time) ÷ F gives moles of electrons.

read.title: Electrons through a wire
text: Drop a strip of zinc into copper(II) sulfate solution and copper metal soon coats the zinc. Zinc atoms hand electrons to Cu²⁺ ions, so zinc is oxidized and the copper ions are reduced. A galvanic cell runs the same reaction with the two halves kept apart. Zinc dips into a zinc salt solution, copper into a copper salt solution, and a wire joins the two metals. Electrons released at the zinc anode travel through the wire to the copper cathode, where Cu²⁺ ions pick them up. A salt bridge lets ions drift between the beakers so that neither solution builds up a charge.

Each half-reaction has a standard reduction potential, measured against the hydrogen electrode, which is set at 0 V. The cell potential is the cathode's value minus the anode's: 0.34 V − (−0.76 V) = +1.10 V. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous, and ΔG° = −nFE°cell turns that voltage into a free energy change. As the cell runs, reactants are used up, the voltage falls as the Nernst equation predicts, and it reaches zero at equilibrium.

An electrolytic cell works the other way. An outside power supply forces a nonspontaneous reaction, such as splitting molten sodium chloride into sodium metal and chlorine gas. The amount of product follows from the charge passed: current times time gives coulombs, and dividing by the Faraday constant, 96,485 C per mole of electrons, gives moles of electrons.
